newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban bomb Masood position north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban bomb Masood position north of Kabul.

text.p: A Taleban plane bombed positions held by former Afghan government troops north of Kabul on Tuesday and five civilians were killed when a Taleban rocket hit the village of Kalakan.

A large cloud of dust rose into the air below the De Sabz pass, 30 km (20 miles) north of the Afghan capital, where bombs struck positions occupied by troops and armour under former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
"It was the Taleban's (warplane)," said one of Masood's commanders. There was no word on casualties.

Masood's forces, along with those of northern Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum's Jumbish-i-Milli faction, have been fighting for several days to try to push the radical Islamic Taleban militia off the De Sabz pass and out of Kabul.
The Afghan capital fell to the Taleban at the end of last month, giving the purist Islamic group control of over two thirds of the country.
Masood's forces had also brought up extra heavy weapons on Tuesday, including four truck-mounted missiles and extra rocket batteries.
But the front line was largely quiet early on Tuesday.
In the village of Kalakan, around 25 km (15 miles) north of Kabul, five people who were killed when a Taleban rocket hit their mud-walled home while they were sleeping early on Tuesday.
Relatives said a further six people had been injured.

A turbaned elder washed the corpse of one man killed in the attack with water from a copper jug. The man, in his thirties, was then wrapped in white linen sheets and an old carpet to prepare for his burial.

Adji Aziz Mohammed, 55, stood impassive next to the bodies of his 40-year-old wife Meloley and his 10-year-old daughter while women cried and chanted nearby over the corpse of his 20-year-old son. One young woman, in an indigo shift, wiped tears from her eyes with a red scarf.
The bent steel tube of the rocket lay in the courtyard of Mohammed's mud-walled compound, crowded with neighbours and family.
"Pakistan is behind this; they want to rule Aghanistan," said Mohammed, citing the widely held belief that the Taleban are backed by neighbouring Pakistan.
Recalling the Soviet invasion in the 1980s, one elderly neighbour said: "The Russians never behaved liked this. They wouldn't have done this."
